text_en: Legal immigration into France should be significantly reduced.
text_generic: Legal immigration should be significantly reduced.
context_en: Legal immigration means foreigners entering the country through regular channels (work, study, family reunification). It is distinct from irregular immigration. Reducing legal immigration means tightening the conditions for obtaining visas or residence permits.
context_generic: Legal immigration means people moving to a country through regular channels: work, study, family or refuge. Cutting it means tighter rules for visas and residence permits. The debate weighs labour needs and family ties against pressure on housing, services and social cohesion.

text_en: Sentences for violent crimes and offences should be made harsher.
text_deck: Violent criminals get off too lightly.
context_en: This is about raising the maximum sentences for violent crimes and offences. Mandatory minimum sentences for repeat offenders existed in France from 2007 to 2014.
context_generic: This is about longer maximum sentences for violent crimes. Supporters say tougher sentences deter offenders and protect the public; critics say the certainty of being caught matters more than the length of the sentence.

text_en: Taxes on the very largest fortunes should be raised.
text_deck: The very rich should pay far more tax.
context_en: France's wealth tax (ISF) was replaced in 2018 by a tax on real estate wealth only (IFI). The question is about taxing large financial and movable fortunes more broadly.
context_generic: A wealth tax is levied on what people own, not what they earn. Supporters say great fortunes grow faster than wages and should contribute more; critics say the rich can move their money abroad and that assets are hard to value.

text_en: The legal retirement age should be lowered.
context_en: The 2023 reform raised France's legal retirement age to 64 and requires 43 years of contributions. The question is about lowering that legal age.
context_generic: As people live longer, pensions cost more, and governments often respond by raising the retirement age. Lowering it means more years of retirement, paid for by higher contributions, higher taxes or lower pensions.

text_en: France should enforce ICC arrest warrants, even against the leaders of allied countries.
text_generic: My country should enforce ICC arrest warrants, even against the leaders of allies.
context_en: The International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague can issue arrest warrants for crimes against humanity, genocide or war crimes, including against the leaders of countries allied with France. France is a party to the Rome Statute, which established the court.
context_generic: The International Criminal Court can issue arrest warrants for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity. Member states are obliged to arrest suspects on their territory, even when the suspect leads a friendly country.

text_en: France should leave the European Union.
text_generic: My country should leave the European Union.
context_en: Article 50 of the Treaty of Lisbon, used by the United Kingdom for Brexit in 2020, sets out how a country leaves the EU. Leaving would mean exiting the single market, the common trade policy and the European legal framework, while keeping the option of negotiating bilateral agreements. About 45% of French exports go to EU member states.
context_generic: Leaving the EU means leaving the single market, the customs union and EU law, and negotiating new trade deals from outside. Supporters stress sovereignty and control over laws and borders; opponents stress trade, jobs and influence.

text_en: Some proportional representation should be introduced in parliamentary elections.
text_generic: Parliamentary seats should be allocated by proportional representation.
text_deck: Every vote should count the same: parliament should be elected by proportional representation.
context_en: France elects its National Assembly by a two-round, single-member majority vote, which favours large parties. Proportional representation would allocate seats according to vote share. A partial system would combine the two.
context_generic: In winner-takes-all systems, each district elects one representative, which favours large parties and usually produces single-party governments. Proportional representation gives parties seats in line with their share of the vote, which tends to mean coalitions.

text_en: The state should hire massively in hospitals and state schools.
text_generic: The state should hire massively in hospitals and schools.
text_deck: Hospitals and schools need an army of new public hires, whatever it costs.
context_en: France has recurring staff shortages in public hospitals and state schools. The question is about large-scale recruitment in these sectors, which means higher public spending.
context_generic: Hiring many more nurses, doctors and teachers means much higher public spending, paid for by taxes or borrowing. Supporters say understaffing costs lives and learning; critics ask where the money and the trained staff will come from.

text_en: The SMIC (minimum wage) should be raised significantly.
text_generic: The minimum wage should be raised significantly.
context_en: The SMIC, France's statutory minimum wage, is set at about €1,443 net per month in 2026. The question is about raising this legal floor significantly; its effects on employment and competitiveness are debated.
context_generic: A statutory minimum wage sets the lowest legal pay. Raising it lifts the incomes of the lowest paid; critics warn it can cost jobs or push up prices if it rises faster than productivity.

text_en: Nuclear power should remain a pillar of French energy policy.
text_generic: Nuclear power should be a pillar of energy policy.
context_en: France generates about 70% of its electricity from nuclear power, one of the highest shares in the world. The debate is over nuclear's place in the energy transition: a low-carbon source of energy sovereignty for some, a technological, financial and waste risk for others.
context_generic: Nuclear power is low-carbon and runs whatever the weather, but brings accident risk, long-lived waste and huge up-front costs. The debate is whether it is a necessary backbone for a low-carbon grid or an expensive detour from renewables.

text_en: Some public services should be opened up to private management.
text_deck: Private companies would run some public services better than the state does.
context_en: Private management of public services can take the form of delegated public service contracts, concessions or privatisation. The debate pits economic efficiency against equal access and continuity of service.
context_generic: Public services can be handed to private operators through contracts, concessions or outright privatisation. Supporters point to efficiency and innovation; critics to profit-taking, unequal access and the risk of services failing.

text_en: France should leave NATO.
text_generic: My country should leave NATO.
context_en: NATO (the North Atlantic Treaty Organization) is a military alliance founded in 1949. France left its integrated military command in 1966 and rejoined it in 2009. Leaving NATO would mean leaving the joint command and its mutual defence guarantees.
context_generic: NATO is a military alliance whose members promise to defend one another if attacked. Leaving means giving up that guarantee and any say in the alliance, in exchange for full independence in defence and foreign policy.

text_en: A citizens' initiative referendum (RIC) should be introduced.
text_generic: Citizens should be able to force a national referendum by collecting signatures.
context_en: The citizens' initiative referendum (RIC) would let a set number of citizens (often around 700,000 signatures) put a question directly to a popular vote, bypassing Parliament and the President.
context_generic: A citizens' initiative lets a set number of voters force a referendum, bypassing parliament. Supporters call it direct democracy; critics say it reduces complex issues to yes or no and favours well-funded campaigns.

text_en: School uniforms should be made compulsory in schools.
context_en: School uniforms are compulsory in many countries (the United Kingdom, Japan, etc.). In France they have been absent from state schools since the Third Republic. The question is about making them compulsory again.
context_generic: Supporters of school uniforms say they hide differences in wealth, reduce peer pressure and build a sense of belonging. Opponents point to the cost for families and the loss of self-expression.

text_en: France should end its subsidies for fossil fuels.
text_generic: Governments should end all subsidies for fossil fuels.
context_en: France spends tens of billions of euros a year supporting fossil fuels, through tax breaks (cheaper off-road diesel, exemptions from domestic fuel tax) and aid to certain industries. The question is about ending all of this public support, for consistency with France's climate targets.
context_generic: Governments support fossil fuels through tax breaks, cheap fuel for particular industries and direct aid. Ending it would align spending with climate goals, but could raise prices for households and hit industries that depend on cheap energy.

text_en: Recreational cannabis should be legalised.
context_en: Recreational cannabis is an illegal drug in France. Regulated legalisation (production, sale and use controlled by the state) exists in several countries (Canada, Uruguay, some US states). It raises public health, tax and anti-trafficking issues.
context_generic: Legalising recreational cannabis means the state regulating its production and sale, as it does alcohol. Supporters cite tax revenue, safer products and less organised crime; opponents cite the health risks, especially for young people.

text_en: France should officially apologise for its colonial past.
text_generic: Former colonial powers should officially apologise for their colonial past.
context_en: France ruled a colonial empire across Africa, Southeast Asia and the Americas from the 17th to the mid-20th century. Crimes were committed during this period: wars of conquest, slavery, the repression of independence movements. Several countries (Belgium, Germany, the Netherlands) have officially apologised for their colonial crimes. France has not yet done so.
context_generic: Colonial empires were built through conquest, slavery and the violent repression of independence movements. Supporters of an apology see it as owed recognition; opponents say today's citizens aren't responsible, or worry about claims for reparations.

text_en: The state should launch a major public investment plan, even at the cost of a larger deficit.
text_deck: Borrow big and build. The deficit can wait.
context_en: Faced with ageing infrastructure, the needs of the green transition and industrial decline, several economists and parties argue for a public investment shock. This Keynesian approach accepts a higher short-term deficit to stimulate the economy and prepare for the future. Others argue that public debt, above 110% of GDP, rules out any further borrowing.
context_generic: The case for: borrow now to repair infrastructure, fund the green transition and revive industry, and growth will pay it back. The case against: more debt means higher interest costs and less room to respond to the next crisis.

text_en: State medical aid (AME) for undocumented migrants should be abolished.
text_generic: Free healthcare for undocumented migrants should be abolished.
context_en: State medical aid (AME) gives foreigners without legal status access to healthcare, subject to income and length-of-stay conditions. It costs about €1 billion a year. The question is about abolishing it.
context_generic: Some countries give undocumented migrants access to routine healthcare; others offer emergency care only. Supporters cite public health and the higher cost of treating illness late; opponents say it encourages irregular migration.

text_en: France should increase its development aid to countries of the Global South.
text_generic: Rich countries should increase their development aid to the Global South.
context_en: French official development assistance (ODA) is about 0.5% of gross national income. The United Nations target is 0.7%. This aid funds health, education and infrastructure projects in developing countries.
context_generic: Development aid funds health, education and infrastructure in poorer countries. Supporters see it as a duty and an investment in stability; critics question whether it works and say the money is needed at home.

text_en: Birthright citizenship should be abolished in France.
text_generic: Birthright citizenship should be abolished.
context_en: Birthright citizenship lets a person born in France to foreign parents obtain French nationality, under certain residence conditions. The question is about abolishing or restricting it, for example by making it depend on the parents' nationality or legal status.
context_generic: Under birthright citizenship, anyone born in a country becomes a citizen. Supporters say it makes children born and raised there full members of society; opponents say citizenship should depend on the parents' status or ties to the country.

text_en: Foreigners without legal status should be systematically deported.
context_en: OQTFs (orders to leave French territory) are administrative removal decisions. Few are actually carried out (about 10–15%). The question is about strengthening deportation of people without legal status.
context_generic: Deportation orders often go unenforced, for lack of travel documents, cooperation from countries of origin, or because of legal appeals. Systematic removal would mean more detention and enforcement, and raises questions about people's rights and ties.

text_en: Foreign residents with legal status should get the right to vote in local elections.
context_en: In France, the right to vote in local elections is reserved for French citizens and EU nationals. Several European countries (Sweden, Denmark, the Netherlands, Portugal) give it to non-EU foreign residents after a few years of legal residence. Introducing it in France would require a constitutional amendment.
context_generic: Some countries let foreign residents vote in local elections after a period of legal residence; others reserve it for citizens. Supporters say those who live and pay taxes somewhere should have a say; opponents say voting should come with citizenship.

text_en: Foreigners should have to wait 5 years before they can receive welfare benefits.
context_en: A waiting period would make access to welfare (minimum income, family allowances, etc.) conditional on a minimum period of legal residence in France. Current waiting periods vary by benefit, from a few months to five years.
context_generic: A waiting period would make access to welfare depend on a minimum length of legal residence. Supporters say it stops welfare from drawing migrants in; critics say it pushes newcomers into poverty.

text_en: Dual French and foreign citizenship should be restricted.
text_generic: Dual citizenship should be restricted.
context_en: Dual citizenship means holding two passports and exercising civic rights in two countries. The question is about restricting it, for example by requiring people to choose a single nationality when they come of age.
context_generic: Dual citizenship means holding two passports and civic rights in two countries. Supporters say it reflects lives lived across borders; critics question divided loyalty. One proposal is to make people choose a single nationality when they come of age.

text_en: Immigrants coming to work should be given priority over others for admission.
text_deck: Let workers in first. Everyone else can wait.
context_en: Immigration to France falls into several categories: work, family reunification, asylum and international protection. The question is about prioritising applications from foreigners coming to work, with faster procedures or easier residence conditions than for other categories.
context_generic: Immigration channels include work, family reunification and asylum. Prioritising labour migrants means faster procedures or easier permits for people with a job or needed skills, and relatively fewer places for everyone else.

text_en: Family reunification should be made easier.
context_en: Family reunification lets a foreigner legally resident in France bring over their spouse and minor children, subject to income and housing conditions. The question is about relaxing or tightening those conditions.
context_generic: Family reunification lets a legally resident foreigner bring over a spouse and children, usually subject to income and housing conditions. The debate is between the right to family life and control over immigration numbers.

text_en: France should take in more asylum seekers.
text_generic: My country should take in more asylum seekers.
context_en: France is bound by the Dublin Regulation, which determines which EU state is responsible for examining an asylum application. The question is about taking in more recognised refugees, notably through relocation schemes within the EU.
context_generic: Asylum is protection for people fleeing persecution or war. Besides those who arrive and claim asylum, countries can resettle refugees directly from abroad. This is about taking in more of both.

text_en: Mandatory minimum sentences for repeat offenders should be brought back.
text_generic: Repeat offenders should face mandatory minimum sentences.
context_en: Mandatory minimums imposed an automatic minimum sentence on repeat offenders, leaving the judge no discretion. Introduced in 2007 and abolished in 2014 in the name of individualised sentencing; the question is about bringing them back.
context_generic: Mandatory minimums set an automatic floor on sentences for repeat offenders, leaving judges no discretion. Supporters say they guarantee firmness; critics say they fill prisons without cutting crime and stop judges weighing each case.

text_en: Juvenile offenders aged 16 and over should be tried as adults.
context_en: The 1945 ordinance on juvenile delinquency put education ahead of punishment for minors. The juvenile criminal justice code, in force since 2021, toughened some provisions. The question is about giving 16- and 17-year-olds the same criminal responsibility as adults.
context_generic: Most justice systems treat young offenders differently, putting education and rehabilitation ahead of punishment. This is about giving 16- and 17-year-olds the same criminal responsibility, and the same sentences, as adults.

text_en: Funded (capitalised) pensions should be developed alongside pay-as-you-go pensions.
text_deck: Part of everyone's pension should be invested in the stock market.
context_en: The French pension system is mainly pay-as-you-go: today's workers' contributions directly fund today's pensions. A funded system instead means saving, individually or collectively (pension funds, retirement savings plans), to pay for one's own future pension. The question is about adding a funded component on top of pay-as-you-go. Supporters present it as a way to top up pensions; opponents cite solidarity between generations and financial market risk.
context_generic: In pay-as-you-go pensions, today's workers fund today's retirees. In funded pensions, people save and invest for their own retirement. Supporters say a funded share boosts pensions; critics cite market risk and weaker solidarity between generations.

text_en: Alternatives to prison (electronic tags, community service, suspended sentences) should be preferred for non-violent offences.
text_deck: Prison is the wrong punishment for non-violent crime.
context_en: France has chronic prison overcrowding: about 75,000 prisoners for 62,000 places in 2025. Alternatives to prison include electronic tagging, community service and suspended sentences. The question is about using them first for non-violent offences, to support rehabilitation and relieve the prisons.
context_generic: Alternatives to prison include electronic tagging, community service and suspended sentences. Supporters cite rehabilitation, cost and overcrowded prisons; critics call them too lenient.

text_en: An independent authority should be created to investigate police violence.
context_en: Violence involving police officers is currently investigated by the General Inspectorate of the National Police (IGPN) and the General Inspectorate of the Gendarmerie (IGGN), which are internal bodies of the ministries concerned. The question is about creating an authority independent of the executive to investigate these cases, like the UK's IOPC or Belgium's Comité P.
context_generic: Complaints against the police are often investigated by the police themselves. An independent body would be separate from both the police and the government. Supporters say only that earns public trust; critics fear it undermines police morale.

text_en: A seat in parliament should be incompatible with any other paid professional activity.
text_deck: Being an MP should be a full-time job, with no side income.
context_en: French members of parliament receive a monthly allowance of about €7,400 gross. They may currently carry on certain professional activities alongside their mandate (liberal professions, company positions, etc.), subject to ethics rules. The question is about a full ban, making a parliamentary seat an exclusive full-time job.
context_generic: Some parliaments let members keep outside jobs alongside their seat. Supporters of a ban say representing people is a full-time job and outside pay creates conflicts of interest; opponents say outside work keeps politicians in touch with the real world.

text_en: More prison places should be built.
context_en: French prisons are chronically overcrowded: about 75,000 prisoners for 62,000 places in 2025. The question is about building new prisons, as opposed to alternatives such as adjusted sentences (electronic tagging, community service).
context_generic: When prisons are overcrowded, the choice is between building more of them and sending fewer people there. Building costs a lot and takes years; sentencing fewer people raises questions of public safety.

text_en: Social media platforms should be held liable for harmful content posted by their users.
context_en: Platforms (Meta, X, TikTok, YouTube) currently enjoy limited liability: they are not treated as publishers of their users' content, which reduces their obligation to act. The EU Digital Services Act (DSA, 2022) introduced new moderation duties for very large platforms. The question is about strengthening their legal liability when they leave up hate speech, disinformation or incitement to violence.
context_generic: Platforms are generally not treated as publishers of what their users post, which limits their legal liability. Making them liable would push them to remove more harmful content, but also, critics fear, more legitimate speech.

text_en: The state should guarantee farmers minimum prices that give them a decent income.
text_deck: Farmers should be guaranteed a price they can live on, whatever the market says.
context_en: Floor prices are guaranteed minimum prices below which farmers cannot sell their produce, intended to cover production costs and their pay. The debate is about the state's role in setting these prices against processors and retailers.
context_generic: A floor price is a guaranteed minimum below which farm produce can't be sold, meant to cover farmers' costs and pay. Supporters say farmers are squeezed by processors and supermarkets; critics warn it can raise food prices or create surpluses.

text_en: An exceptional levy should be introduced on inheritances above €2 million.
text_deck: Nobody should inherit a fortune without paying extra for it.
context_en: French inheritance tax is progressive, depending on family relationship and the amount inherited. For direct descendants it reaches 45% above €1.8 million. The question is about an additional levy targeting the very largest estates, to redistribute wealth between generations.
context_generic: Inheritance taxes are usually progressive, and often lower for close family. Supporters say large inheritances entrench inequality from one generation to the next; opponents see taxing them as punishing families for passing on what they built.

text_en: Employer social security contributions should be cut.
text_deck: Employers pay too much to hire people.
context_en: Employer contributions fund social security (health, pensions, workplace accidents, unemployment). The question is about cutting them to lower labour costs; their effects on employment and on funding social protection are debated.
context_generic: Employers pay contributions on wages that fund social protection: health, pensions, unemployment. Cutting them lowers the cost of hiring; the question is how the lost funding would be replaced.

text_en: Companies that received public aid should not be allowed to relocate abroad for 10 years.
text_deck: Take public money, and you don't get to move the jobs abroad.
context_en: National and local government give companies several billion euros of aid each year: subsidies, tax exemptions, subsidised loans, equity stakes. The question is about a clause making this support conditional on not relocating activities for 10 years.
context_generic: Governments give companies subsidies, tax breaks and cheap loans. This would attach a condition: take the money, and you can't move jobs abroad for 10 years. Supporters call it fair; critics say it would scare off investment.

text_en: Strategic sectors (energy, transport) should be nationalised.
text_deck: Energy and transport should belong to the state.
context_en: Nationalisation transfers ownership of private companies to the state in sectors considered strategic. EDF was fully renationalised in 2023. The question is about extending this to other sectors (water, transport, telecoms, banks).
context_generic: Nationalisation moves private companies into state ownership. Supporters say strategic sectors like energy and transport should serve the public, not shareholders; critics point to cost, inefficiency and political meddling.

text_en: France should be able to override the European Convention on Human Rights to pursue its migration policy.
text_generic: My country should be able to override European human rights rulings to enforce its migration policy.
context_en: The European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), signed in 1950, guarantees among other things the right to private and family life and prohibits inhuman or degrading treatment. The European Court of Human Rights has several times halted deportations ordered by the French authorities. The question is about France being able to disregard these rulings when removing people from its territory.
context_generic: The European Convention on Human Rights protects family life and bans inhuman or degrading treatment, and its court can halt deportations. This is about letting a government set those rulings aside on migration, at the cost of weakening the convention.

text_en: France should commit to a process of nuclear disarmament.
text_generic: Nuclear-armed states should commit to nuclear disarmament.
context_en: France has a nuclear deterrent of ballistic missile submarines and air-launched missiles, about 290 warheads. It is one of the five nuclear powers officially recognised by the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT). France has not signed the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW), which came into force in 2021.
context_generic: Nuclear disarmament means giving up nuclear weapons, gradually or by treaty. Supporters say they threaten catastrophe; opponents say deterrence keeps the peace between major powers and that disarming alone leaves a country exposed.

text_en: The sale of new petrol and diesel cars should be banned by 2035.
context_en: In 2023 the European Union adopted a ban on selling new combustion-engine cars from 2035, with an exemption for carbon-neutral synthetic fuels. The question is about keeping or relaxing that deadline.
context_generic: Banning new petrol and diesel cars forces a switch to electric and other low-emission vehicles. Supporters say it gives industry a clear target; critics cite cost, charging infrastructure and the impact on carmakers and rural drivers.

text_en: A universal basic income should be introduced.
context_en: A universal basic income would be paid to all adults unconditionally, regardless of income or employment. Its amount (often proposed at around €800–1,000 a month) and how to fund it (overhauling existing benefits, raising taxes) are widely debated.
context_generic: A universal basic income would pay every adult a fixed sum, with no means test and no work requirement. How much, how to fund it, and whether people would still work are the big arguments.

text_en: VAT on essential goods should be abolished.
text_deck: Food and soap shouldn't be taxed at all.
context_en: VAT on basic foodstuffs is already at a reduced rate of 5.5% in France. The question is about scrapping it entirely for a list of essentials (basic food, hygiene products), to make it less regressive.
context_generic: Sales taxes like VAT fall hardest on poorer households, who spend more of what they earn. Scrapping them on essentials like food and hygiene products helps those households, but the rich save money too and the state loses revenue.

text_en: The legal working week should be raised above 35 hours.
text_generic: The legal working week should be longer.
text_deck: The standard working week is too short.
context_en: France's legal working week has been 35 hours since 2000. Above that threshold, overtime is paid at a premium (25% to 50% extra). The question is about raising the legal threshold above 35 hours, not just about tax breaks on overtime.
context_generic: The legal working week sets the hours above which overtime pay kicks in, or caps hours outright. A longer week could raise output and lower labour costs; opponents cite health, family life and fewer jobs to go round.

text_en: The right to strike in public services should be limited.
context_en: The right to strike is guaranteed by the French Constitution. A legally mandated minimum service has existed in air transport since 2012. The question is about extending that obligation to other public services (land transport, hospitals, schools) to guarantee a minimum of continuity.
context_generic: The right to strike is a basic protection for workers, but strikes in public services hit the people who depend on them. Limiting it could mean a guaranteed minimum service, longer notice, or bans in essential sectors.

text_en: Assisted reproduction should be fully reimbursed and access to it widened (age, medical criteria).
context_en: Assisted reproduction (PMA) was opened to lesbian couples and single women by the 2021 bioethics law. It is still subject to age limits and only partly reimbursed by social security. The question is about full reimbursement and wider access criteria.
context_generic: Assisted reproduction (IVF and related treatments) is often limited by age, medical criteria, waiting lists and partial funding, and access for single women and same-sex couples varies. This is about full public funding and wider access.

text_en: Surrogacy should be legalised in France.
text_generic: Surrogacy should be legal.
context_en: Surrogacy is banned in France. It means a woman carries a child for another couple, to whom she hands it over at birth. The debate covers the commodification of the body, equal rights between couples and the protection of children born through surrogacy abroad.
context_generic: In surrogacy, a woman carries a child for another person or couple and hands it over at birth. The debate covers commodification of the body, the rights of the surrogate, equal rights for couples, and the interests of the child.

text_en: The right to assisted dying (medical help to end one's life) should be legalised in France.
text_generic: Assisted dying should be legal.
context_en: Assisted dying (euthanasia or assisted suicide) is legal in several countries (the Netherlands, Belgium, Switzerland, Canada). In France, the 2016 Claeys-Leonetti law allows deep sedation but not active assistance in dying. A specific bill was debated in 2024–2025.
context_generic: Assisted dying means helping a terminally ill or suffering person end their life, through euthanasia or assisted suicide. Supporters cite autonomy and dignity; opponents fear pressure on vulnerable people and a slippery slope.

text_en: Access to abortion should be made easier and wider.
context_en: The right to abortion has been guaranteed in France since the 1975 law and was written into the Constitution in 2024. The legal limit is 14 weeks. The question is about extending the time limit, regional access and reimbursement.
context_generic: Abortion laws vary in time limits, cost and ease of access. This is about longer time limits, better local access and full public funding. The debate turns on bodily autonomy and on when the unborn should be protected.

text_en: A progressive carbon tax should be introduced on plane tickets.
text_deck: The more you fly, the more tax you should pay per ticket.
context_en: Aviation accounts for 2–3% of global CO₂ emissions, not counting altitude effects that amplify its climate impact. In France, plane tickets carry a solidarity levy (the Chirac tax) with a fixed amount by destination and class. The question is about a tax that rises with distance and how often people fly, to discourage air travel.
context_generic: Aviation is a significant and fast-growing source of emissions, and a small share of frequent flyers takes most flights. A progressive tax would rise with distance and with how often you fly.

text_en: The governance of large companies should be shared equally between shareholder and employee representatives.
text_deck: Workers should have as many seats on the board as shareholders.
context_en: In France, employees are represented on the boards of large companies, but as a minority (1 or 2 seats depending on size). In Germany, co-determination (Mitbestimmung) requires parity on the supervisory boards of companies with more than 2,000 employees. The question is about adopting a similar model in France.
context_generic: In most companies, shareholders elect the board. Co-determination gives employees seats too; parity means half of them. Supporters say it leads to longer-term decisions; critics say it slows companies down and deters investors.

text_en: Strict rent controls should be introduced in big cities.
context_en: Rent control sets a reference rent per area and type of housing, with a legal ceiling. It has been trialled in several large French cities since 2019. The question is about extending it nationally or to all high-pressure housing areas.
context_generic: Rent control caps rents or rent rises. Supporters say it protects tenants from being priced out; critics say it discourages building and maintenance and shrinks the supply of homes to rent.

text_en: Procedures for economic redundancies should be simplified.
text_deck: It should be easier to lay people off.
context_en: In France, economic redundancies follow strict procedures: consulting employee representatives, drawing up a job-protection plan (PSE) in large companies, and oversight by the labour inspectorate. The question is about simplifying them so companies can adapt faster to economic change, at the risk of weakening employee protection.
context_generic: Laying off staff for economic reasons often involves consultation, notice periods, severance pay and sometimes official approval. Simplifying that lets companies adapt faster, at the cost of weaker protection for employees.

text_en: The carbon tax should be raised.
context_en: The carbon tax (climate-energy contribution) raises the price of fossil fuels (motor fuel, heating oil) to encourage lower CO₂ emissions. In France, its planned increases were frozen in 2018 after major social protests.
context_generic: A carbon tax raises the price of fossil fuels to cut emissions. It hits drivers and rural households hardest and can spark protests; some designs return the revenue to households as a rebate.

text_en: Factory farming should be phased out.
context_en: Intensive livestock farming concentrates large numbers of animals in small spaces to cut production costs. The question is about phasing it out on grounds of animal welfare and environmental impact (soil and water pollution, antibiotic use).
context_generic: Intensive livestock farming keeps large numbers of animals in small spaces to cut costs. Phasing it out would improve animal welfare and reduce pollution, but raise the price of meat, eggs and milk.

text_en: Pesticides should be phased out.
context_en: Synthetic pesticides (including glyphosate) are debated for their health and environmental effects. France has launched plans to reduce their use (the Écophyto plan). The question is about a gradual, general ban.
context_generic: Synthetic pesticides raise yields but are contested for their effects on health, insects and water. A general ban would mean a shift to organic or low-input farming, with lower yields or higher costs.

text_en: Bullfighting should be banned in France.
context_en: Bullfighting is legal in French towns with an unbroken bullfighting tradition, mainly in the south-west and some Mediterranean towns. It is exempt from the 1963 animal protection law. The question pits those who defend it as cultural heritage against those who see it as animal cruelty incompatible with contemporary values.

text_en: Renewable energy should make up 100% of the electricity mix by 2050.
context_en: Generating 100% of electricity from renewables (solar, wind, hydro, biomass) requires solving intermittency (storage, grid balancing). Reaching this by 2050 means a deep transformation of the generating fleet.
context_generic: A fully renewable grid runs on sun, wind, water and biomass. The challenge is intermittency: storing power and balancing the grid when there is no sun or wind. Getting there means rebuilding the whole generating fleet.

text_en: France should stop building new motorways.
text_generic: No new motorways should be built.
context_en: France has a motorway network of about 12,000 km, one of the densest in Europe. Several new motorway projects are being studied or tendered. The question pits supporters of mobility and opening up remote areas against environmentalists, who point to land take and the CO₂ emitted by building and using motorways.
context_generic: Supporters say new motorways connect remote areas, ease congestion and help the economy. Opponents say they pave over land and generate more traffic and emissions, and that the money should go to public transport.

text_en: National defence spending should reach 3% of GDP.
context_en: French defence spending is about 2% of GDP, in line with the NATO target. The question is about raising it to 3%, a substantial increase in military spending.
context_generic: Defence spending is usually measured as a share of GDP. Raising it means more equipment, more recruits and more readiness for war; the money has to come from taxes, borrowing or other budgets.

text_en: A windfall tax should be introduced on the excess profits of oil companies.
text_deck: Oil companies' crisis profits should be taxed away.
context_en: A windfall tax targets exceptional profits made during a crisis, notably by oil and gas companies during the 2022–2023 energy crisis. Several European countries introduced one temporarily over that period.
context_generic: A windfall tax targets exceptional profits made because of a crisis, like soaring energy prices. Supporters call those profits unearned; critics say such taxes deter investment and change the rules after the fact.

text_en: France should step up its military support for Ukraine.
text_generic: My country should step up its military support for Ukraine.
context_en: Since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, France has provided military aid (artillery, armoured vehicles, training). The question is about intensifying this support, particularly heavy weapons and funding.
context_generic: Military support means weapons, ammunition, training and funding. Supporters say it defends a country against invasion and deters further aggression; critics fear escalation and the cost.

text_en: Controls at the EU's external borders should be tightened.
context_en: The Frontex agency monitors the Schengen area's external borders. The question is about tightening controls at the EU's external borders, particularly in the Mediterranean and on land borders, to limit irregular entry.
context_generic: The EU's external borders are the frontiers of the passport-free Schengen area, so what happens there affects every member. Tighter controls mean more patrols, fences and checks, and raise questions about how people seeking asylum are treated.

text_en: France should develop a common European army.
text_generic: The EU should build a common European army.
context_en: A common European army would mean a unified military command among EU member states, separate from NATO. It would involve partially transferring defence sovereignty and a common budget. Several member states are reluctant.
context_generic: A European army would mean a unified command of member states' forces, with a shared budget and a partial transfer of sovereignty over defence. Supporters say Europe must be able to defend itself; opponents prize national control.

text_en: The RSA (minimum income) should remain conditional on mandatory hours of activity or volunteering.
text_generic: Welfare benefits should be conditional on mandatory hours of work or volunteering.
context_en: The RSA (active solidarity income) is paid to people with resources below about €635 a month for a single person. In 2024 the government made 15 hours a week of activity (work, training or volunteering) compulsory for recipients. The left wants to repeal this in the name of unconditional welfare; the right wants to keep or strengthen it.
context_generic: Welfare conditions can include job-search requirements or compulsory hours of work, training or volunteering. Supporters say rights come with duties; critics say conditions push the most vulnerable out of support.

text_en: France should maintain diplomatic relations with Russia.
text_generic: My country should maintain diplomatic relations with Russia.
context_en: Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, triggering EU economic sanctions and a freeze in diplomatic relations with many Western countries. France has kept some channels of communication with Moscow open. The question is about maintaining diplomatic relations with Russia, weighing the need for dialogue to resolve the conflict against the risk of legitimising Russian aggression.
context_generic: Keeping diplomatic relations means keeping embassies and channels of dialogue open. The case for is that talking is the only path to peace; the case against is that it legitimises aggression.

text_en: Facial recognition should be banned in public spaces.
context_en: Facial recognition uses algorithms to identify people from their physical features, live or after the fact. In France, police use is limited, but the 2024 Olympic Games revived the debate over deploying it in public spaces. The EU AI Act (2024) strictly regulates it. The question is about a total ban to protect privacy and individual freedoms.
context_generic: Facial recognition identifies people from their faces, live or from recordings. Police say it helps catch suspects; critics say it enables mass surveillance and misidentifies people. This is about a total ban in public places.

text_en: France should reduce its military presence in Africa.
context_en: France maintains military bases and pre-positioned forces in several sub-Saharan African countries. Since 2022, several states (Mali, Niger, Burkina Faso, Chad, Senegal) have asked French troops to leave. The question is about reducing or ending this presence.

text_en: Taxation should be harmonised across EU countries to prevent tax competition between states.
context_en: Some EU states tax companies very lightly to attract corporate headquarters (Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands). European tax harmonisation would set a common minimum rate on profits, limiting competition between member states.
context_generic: Some EU countries tax companies very lightly to attract their headquarters. Harmonisation would set common rules or a minimum rate on profits across the EU, limiting competition between member states.

text_en: France should move to a Sixth Republic.
text_generic: My country needs a new constitution.
context_en: The Fifth Republic, founded in 1958, is characterised by a strong presidential executive. Moving to a Sixth Republic would mean adopting a new constitution that rebalances power between the President, the government and Parliament.
context_generic: A constitution sets how power is shared between head of state, government, parliament and courts. Writing a new one is a way to reset a political system; critics say it distracts from fixing concrete problems.

text_en: Article 49.3 of the Constitution should be abolished.
text_generic: Governments should not be able to pass laws without a vote in parliament.
context_en: Article 49.3 of the Constitution lets the government stake its survival on a budget or social security financing bill, which is then adopted without a vote unless a motion of no confidence is tabled and passed within 24 hours. It has been used many times, notably during the 2024 budget debate. Critics call it undemocratic; defenders see it as necessary for government stability.
context_generic: Some constitutions let a government force a bill through without a final vote, daring parliament to bring it down instead. Critics call such tools undemocratic; defenders say they keep minority governments stable.

text_en: Parliament should be given more power relative to the executive.
context_en: Article 49.3 of the French Constitution lets the government pass a bill without a vote unless a motion of no confidence is passed within 24 hours. The question is about reducing the executive's powers and strengthening the role of Parliament.
context_generic: The balance between parliament and the executive varies. Where governments control the agenda, rely on emergency powers or rule by decree, parliament can become a rubber stamp. This is about shifting power back to parliament.

text_en: The state should be able to requisition empty homes to tackle the housing crisis.
text_deck: The state should be able to seize empty homes to house people.
context_en: France has about 3 million vacant homes, some deliberately left empty by their owners. The right of requisition has existed in law since the 1982 Quilliot law but is very rarely used. The housing crisis shows up as long waiting lists for social housing and soaring rents in big cities. The question is about actually using requisition to house homeless people or those in severe hardship.
context_generic: Cities often have homes standing empty while people sleep rough or wait years for social housing. Requisition lets the state take temporary control of empty homes to house people. Critics see it as an attack on property rights.

text_en: Farm subsidies should be conditional on strict environmental standards.
text_deck: No farm subsidies without strict environmental rules.
context_en: The EU Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) pays subsidies to European farmers, largely based on farm area. Strict environmental conditionality would tie these payments to agro-ecological practices (hedgerows, crop rotation, reduced pesticide use).
context_generic: Farm subsidies are often paid per hectare or per unit produced, regardless of how the land is farmed. Strict conditions would tie them to practices like hedgerows, crop rotation and less pesticide.

text_en: Conspicuous religious symbols should be banned for everyone in public services, staff and users alike.
context_en: In France, a 2004 law bans pupils at state schools from wearing conspicuous religious symbols (headscarf, kippah, large cross). Public servants are bound by religious neutrality. The question is about extending the ban to the users of public services.
context_generic: Some countries require strict religious neutrality in public life; others allow religious symbols freely. This is about banning conspicuous symbols (headscarf, kippah, large cross) for staff and users of public services alike.

text_en: Menstrual leave should be introduced and paid for by social security.
text_generic: Menstrual leave should be introduced and paid for by the state.
context_en: Endometriosis and severe period pain affect about 10% of women of reproductive age and are a frequent cause of absence from work. In 2023 Spain introduced three days a month of menstrual leave, paid by social security. The question is about a similar scheme in France, letting women with disabling pain take time off without loss of pay.
context_generic: Severe period pain, including endometriosis, is a common cause of missed work. Menstrual leave would allow paid days off without loss of pay. Supporters call it overdue; critics fear it could make employers wary of hiring women.

text_en: The state should strengthen and increase funding for public broadcasting (France Télévisions, Radio France).
text_generic: Public broadcasting should get more public funding.
context_en: France Télévisions, Radio France and France Médias Monde have been funded from the state budget since the licence fee was abolished in 2022. The question is about increasing this public funding to strengthen public broadcasting.
context_generic: Public broadcasters are funded by a licence fee or directly from the state budget. Supporters say they provide independent news and culture the market won't; critics question paying for them and their neutrality.

text_en: Sex education should be strengthened and made compulsory from primary school to the end of secondary school.
context_en: Since 2001, French law has provided for three sessions a year of sex and relationships education from primary school to the end of secondary school. In practice these sessions rarely happen, for lack of teacher training and resources. The question is about actually strengthening this teaching, including consent, gender equality and reproductive health.
context_generic: Sex education ranges from none at all to a compulsory curriculum from primary school. This is about making it thorough and compulsory, including consent, gender equality and reproductive health. Some parents want to decide this themselves.

text_en: A legal maximum income should be introduced.
text_deck: Nobody should be allowed to earn more than a legal maximum.
context_en: A legal maximum income would set a ceiling above which any additional income (salary, dividends, capital income) is taxed away entirely by the state. Several proposals have been made in France, with ceilings ranging from 36 times the minimum wage to 20 times the median salary (about €400,000 a year). This is distinct from simply raising the top marginal tax rate: it is an absolute legal ceiling.
context_generic: A legal maximum income would tax away all income above a ceiling, often set as a multiple of the minimum or median wage. It is an absolute cap, not just a higher top tax rate.

text_en: The law should limit concentrated ownership of news media.
text_deck: No single owner should control too much of the news.
context_en: In France, several large industrial or financial groups own television channels, radio stations, newspapers and online media at the same time. The question is about introducing or strengthening anti-concentration rules limiting how many media outlets one shareholder can control, to protect media pluralism.
context_generic: When a few owners control many TV channels, radio stations, newspapers and news sites, they can shape public debate. Anti-concentration rules cap how much media one owner can control, in the name of pluralism.

text_en: School catchment areas should be abolished so families can freely choose their school.
text_deck: Parents should be free to pick any school, not the one they're assigned.
context_en: The carte scolaire assigns pupils to a state school based on where they live. It aims to ensure a degree of social mix but is often circumvented by better-off families. The question is about abolishing it entirely, letting all families freely choose a state school in or outside their area, at the risk of widening inequalities between schools.
context_generic: Catchment areas assign children to a public school by where they live, aiming for a social mix, though better-off families often get round them by moving. Abolishing them would let every family choose, at the risk of widening gaps between schools.

text_en: France's overseas territories should be given more institutional autonomy.
context_en: France's overseas territories (overseas departments, regions and collectivities) have varied institutional statuses. Some want more legislative autonomy to adapt rules to their local, especially economic and social, realities. This would require a constitutional amendment.

text_en: The voting age should be lowered to 16.
context_en: In France, the voting age is 18. Several European countries (Austria, Malta, Scotland, Germany for some elections) have lowered it to 16. A bill to that effect has been debated in the National Assembly. Supporters point to young people's civic engagement; opponents think the voting age should stay aligned with the legal age of majority.
context_generic: Supporters of votes at 16 say young people live longest with today's decisions and that voting early builds the habit. Opponents say voting should match the age of legal adulthood.

text_en: Minimum welfare benefits (RSA, AAH) should be raised significantly.
text_generic: Minimum welfare benefits should be raised significantly.
context_en: The RSA (minimum income) is about €635 a month for a single person in 2026. The AAH (disabled adults' allowance) is about €1,016 a month. Both are below the French poverty line of about €1,100. The question is about raising these benefits significantly so recipients can meet their basic needs.
context_generic: The lowest welfare benefits often sit below the poverty line. Raising them significantly would help recipients cover their basic needs; critics worry about the cost and about reducing the incentive to work.

text_en: The Universal National Service (SNU) should be made compulsory.
text_generic: National service should be compulsory for young people.
context_en: The Universal National Service (SNU) has been trialled on a voluntary basis since 2019 for 15- to 17-year-olds. It includes a two-week residential stay and a public-interest assignment. The question is about making it compulsory for everyone in that age group.
context_generic: National service means a period of compulsory military or civilian service for young people. Supporters say it builds cohesion, skills and readiness; opponents object to the compulsion and the cost.

text_en: Social security should cover 100% of healthcare costs.
text_generic: Public health insurance should cover 100% of healthcare costs.
context_en: French social security reimburses on average 77% of health spending. The rest is covered by top-up insurers (mutuelles), which are unequally affordable depending on income. The question is about 100% reimbursement by social security.
context_generic: Health systems differ in how much patients pay themselves, through fees, co-payments and private insurance. This is about the public system covering everything, paid for through taxes or contributions.

text_en: Medical deserts should be tackled by creating public health centres with salaried doctors.
text_deck: Doctor shortages should be fixed with public clinics and salaried doctors.
context_en: Medical deserts are areas where there are too few doctors to meet the population's needs. About 6 million French people have no regular GP. Health centres employ salaried doctors, unlike self-employed private practices. The question is about making these public centres the main response to unequal access to care in under-served areas.
context_generic: Many rural and poor areas lack doctors. Public health centres employ salaried doctors instead of relying on self-employed doctors choosing where to work. This is about making them the main answer.

text_en: Parcoursup should be abolished.
context_en: Parcoursup is the national platform for applying to higher education, launched in 2018. It ranks applications according to criteria set by each institution. The question is about replacing it with another allocation method (lottery, priority for baccalauréat holders, etc.).

text_en: France should recognise a third, neutral gender marker on civil status documents.
text_generic: Official documents should offer a third, neutral gender marker.
context_en: French civil status records recognise two sexes: male or female. Some trans and non-binary people call for a third marker, often X or neutral. Germany, the Netherlands and several other countries have introduced this option. The reform would require amending the French Civil Code.
context_generic: Official documents usually record only male or female. A third option, often marked X, would recognise non-binary and some intersex people. Opponents say sex should be recorded as a biological fact.

text_en: Motorways should be renationalised.
text_generic: Toll motorways should be brought back into public ownership.
context_en: French motorways were conceded to private companies (Vinci Autoroutes, Eiffage, Abertis) between 1990 and 2006. The concessions expire between 2031 and 2036. Renationalisation would bring ownership and management of this infrastructure back into public hands.
context_generic: Some motorways are run by private companies under long concessions, funded by tolls. Bringing them back into public ownership would end private profits from them, but the state would carry the cost of running them.

text_en: Advertising for unhealthy products (alcohol, tobacco, junk food) should be further restricted.
context_en: Alcohol advertising is regulated by a 1991 law that allows certain messages in certain media. Tobacco advertising has been almost entirely banned since 1991. The question is about tightening these restrictions and extending them to junk food and sugary drinks.
context_generic: Advertising for tobacco and alcohol is already restricted in many places. This is about tightening the rules and extending them to junk food and sugary drinks. Critics see it as the nanny state.

text_en: More social housing should be built.
context_en: France has about 5 million social housing units (HLM), run by public or semi-public bodies. Given the housing crisis and long waiting lists, the question is about a major programme to build new social housing.
context_generic: Social housing is rented below market rates, usually by public or non-profit landlords. Building much more of it would cut waiting lists and rents, but takes significant public investment.

text_en: The state should be able to block social media in case of public disorder.
context_en: In 2023, during the riots after the death of Nahel Merzouk, the government raised the possibility of restricting access to social media to limit coordination of violence. TikTok, Snapchat and Twitter (X) were particularly targeted. The question is about a legal framework letting the state temporarily block these services, in tension with freedom of expression and the right to information.
context_generic: During unrest, social media can be used to coordinate violence. A legal power to block these services temporarily could help keep order, but is in tension with free expression and the right to information.

text_en: Landlords should find it easier to evict tenants who don't pay their rent.
context_en: Eviction proceedings take more than a year on average in France, and all evictions are suspended during the winter truce from 1 November to 31 March. The question is about simplifying and speeding up these procedures for landlords.
context_generic: Evicting a tenant for unpaid rent can take many months. Faster evictions protect landlords' income and may encourage letting; critics say they push vulnerable people into homelessness.

text_en: A tax should be introduced on fast fashion (cheap clothing produced abroad).
context_en: Fast fashion means cheap clothing produced in large quantities, often in low-wage countries. A law passed in France in 2024 provides for a tax on very cheap clothing produced abroad, to internalise its environmental and social costs.
context_generic: Fast fashion is cheap clothing made in large volumes, often in low-wage countries, and thrown away quickly. A tax would make prices reflect its environmental and social costs, but hit people on low incomes hardest.

text_en: France should recognise the crime of ecocide in its criminal law.
text_generic: Ecocide should be a crime under national law.
context_en: Ecocide means the massive, deliberate destruction of a natural ecosystem. The Citizens' Convention for Climate (2020) recommended writing it into the French Constitution, but the proposal did not go through. In 2024 the International Criminal Court extended its remit to serious environmental crimes. The question is about creating a crime of ecocide in French criminal law, so those responsible for major environmental destruction can be prosecuted.
context_generic: Ecocide means the massive, deliberate destruction of an ecosystem. Making it a crime would let executives and officials be prosecuted for major environmental damage.

text_en: Building in protected areas should be made easier to meet housing needs.
text_deck: Protected land should be opened up for housing.
context_en: Protected areas (Natura 2000 sites, wetlands, sensitive natural areas) are subject to strict planning rules that limit construction. Given the housing crisis, the question is about relaxing these rules to allow more building in these areas.
context_generic: Protected areas, like nature reserves, wetlands and green belts, have strict building rules. With housing short, this is about relaxing them to allow more construction.
